topic.subject: social
topic.title: The age of industrialisation
topic.scope: proto-industrialisation, factories, hand labour vs machines, Indian textiles, industrialists, advertising

misconceptions.statement: Proto-industrialisation was just a small-scale version of the modern factory system.
misconceptions.why: Students often assume industrial history is a linear progression where factories simply grew larger over time.
misconceptions.fix: Proto-industrialisation relied on a decentralized network of rural households working for merchants, whereas factories centralize production under one roof.

probe.question: How did production in the proto-industrial phase differ from the factory system?
probe.wrong_answer: It was the same, just with fewer machines and smaller buildings.

misconceptions.statement: The proto-industrial system was inefficient and disappeared immediately when factories arrived.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often focus on the triumph of the factory, leading students to believe older systems vanished instantly.
misconceptions.fix: Hand production continued to coexist with factories for a long time because machines could not produce intricate designs or meet fluctuating market demands.

probe.question: What happened to rural weavers once factories were established in England?
probe.wrong_answer: They all immediately lost their jobs and moved to cities to work in factories.

misconceptions.statement: Industrialists always preferred machines because they were cheaper and faster.
misconceptions.why: Students equate 'industrialization' with 'automation' and assume machines are always the superior economic choice.
misconceptions.fix: Industrialists often preferred hand labour because machines were expensive, prone to breakdown, and could not produce the specific, varied designs demanded by the elite.

probe.question: Why did many Victorian industrialists hesitate to introduce new steam-powered machines?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they were not smart enough to understand the new technology.

misconceptions.statement: Indian textiles were inferior to British machine-made goods, which is why they lost the market.
misconceptions.why: Students often conflate 'machine-made' with 'better quality' due to modern branding.
misconceptions.fix: Indian textiles were highly prized for their quality and design; they lost the market due to high import duties and colonial policies that favored British manufacturers.

probe.question: Why did Indian weavers struggle to compete with British textiles?
probe.wrong_answer: Because Indian cloth was of poor quality compared to the perfect machine-made cloth from Britain.

misconceptions.statement: Advertising was only used to inform people about the technical features of a new product.
misconceptions.why: Students view advertising through a modern, rational lens rather than as a tool for cultural influence.
misconceptions.fix: Advertising was used to create emotional connections, build brand loyalty, and associate products with nationalistic or imperial pride.

probe.question: Why did manufacturers put images of Indian gods on labels of imported cloth?
probe.wrong_answer: To explain the technical specifications of the cloth to the buyers.
